incidents.title: United States: Justice Department investigates the Chicago Tribune under the Espionage Act over Battle of Midway coverage
incidents.summary: The United States Department of Justice convened a federal grand jury to consider Espionage Act charges against the Chicago Tribune and correspondent Stanley Johnston after the newspaper published details suggesting the Navy had broken Japanese naval codes ahead of the Battle of Midway. The grand jury declined to return an indictment.
incidents.what_happened: On June 7, 1942, the Chicago Tribune published a dispatch by war correspondent Stanley Johnston reporting that the United States Navy had known in advance of Japanese plans for the Battle of Midway, detail that closely tracked a secret dispatch Admiral Chester W. Nimitz, commander of the Pacific Fleet, had sent to his commanders on May 31. The article's account of the Japanese fleet's organization suggested that American codebreakers had penetrated Japanese naval communications, one of the most closely held secrets of the war. The Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Department of Justice, and the Navy examined whether Johnston and the Tribune had violated the Espionage Act of 1917 by publishing the leaked classified information. By August 1942, the Department of Justice had convened a federal grand jury in Chicago, hearing testimony from naval officers and editors of other newspapers that had run the story. The grand jury ultimately declined to issue any indictment, avoiding a public trial in which the government feared exposing to Japan that its codes had been broken.
incidents.stated_justification: Federal investigators viewed the article as damaging national security by indirectly revealing that the United States had penetrated Japan's naval codes.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The grand jury's decision not to indict was heralded as a great First Amendment victory by the Tribune and other news media.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The Battle of Midway, fought in early June 1942, was a major turning point in the Pacific war, and the United States guarded its codebreaking success as one of the most sensitive secrets of the conflict.
incidents.outcome_note: The federal grand jury investigating the Tribune and Johnston declined to issue any indictment.

incidents.title: Greece: collaborationist government creates a Directorate-General for Press and Radio to review films and publications before release
incidents.jurisdiction: Greece, national, under Axis military occupation
incidents.summary: The collaborationist government installed in occupied Greece created a Directorate-General for Press and Radio to take over and expand the prior review powers of the prewar Metaxas dictatorship, requiring official permission before films, plays, music, and publications could reach the public. German Embassy officials reviewed the same material and could overrule the Greek reviewers.
incidents.what_happened: Germany and Italy, joined by Bulgarian and Hungarian units, occupied Greece beginning April 6, 1941, and divided the country into occupation zones. The Germans installed a collaborationist government, and on May 8, 1941, a legal decree issued by the Tsolakoglou government transferred the prior-review powers of the prewar Under-Secretariat for Press and Tourism to a new Directorate-General for Press and Radio, set up as an office under the government's president. In 1942 and 1943, Legal Decree 1108 and Law 485 put review of films, theater, music, and publications on a more systematic legal footing. Film distribution companies had to apply to the Directorate-General's People's Enlightenment Directorate for a license to screen any picture, attaching a plot summary and script. German Embassy officials attended pre-screenings and could reject a film outright; surviving licensing files carry handwritten notes recording that a film had been prohibited or that its license had been granted by the German Embassy.
incidents.stated_justification: The decree establishing the Directorate-General stated that it was meant to enlighten public opinion on Greek affairs and to elevate the national and religious spirit of the Greek people.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Licensing files show that the Greek censors' decisions were routinely subject to a separate German Embassy review, with applications marked as prohibited or approved by the German Embassy.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The film and publication review apparatus operated during the Axis occupation of Greece, which began in April 1941 when Germany, Italy, and Bulgaria divided the country into occupation zones.
incidents.outcome_note: The Directorate-General continued to license and review films and publications, with German Embassy oversight, through the years covered by its surviving archive.

incidents.title: Canada: War Measures Act regulations authorize review of hundreds of newspapers and ban political organizations
incidents.summary: Canada invoked the War Measures Act at the outset of the Second World War and used it to bring in the Defence of Canada Regulations, which gave the government power to review and restrict hundreds of newspapers and periodicals and to ban dozens of organizations, including the Communist Party of Canada.
incidents.what_happened: The War Measures Act was invoked again for the Second World War and took effect on August 25, 1939, one week before Canada's own declaration against Germany. Cabinet used the Act to bring in the Defence of Canada Regulations, which were implemented on September 3, 1939. The Regulations gave authorities power to review and restrict 325 newspapers and periodicals and to ban more than 30 religious, cultural, and political organizations, including Jehovah's Witnesses and the Communist Party of Canada. They also let the Minister of Justice detain, without due process, anyone who acted in a manner prejudicial to public safety or the safety of the state, and free speech was restricted as a result. Montreal's mayor, Camillien Houde, was arrested at city hall in 1940 and interned for four years in Ontario for denouncing government conscription policy. The Communist Party of Canada was itself banned the following year, and more than 100 of its leading members were imprisoned. The wartime Regulations remained in force until they were replaced by similar legislation on December 31, 1945.
incidents.stated_justification: The Regulations let the Minister of Justice detain, without due process, anyone who acted in a manner prejudicial to public safety or the safety of the state, the standard the government invoked to justify wartime press restrictions and internment.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Free speech was restricted and anyone critical of government positions risked internment without charge or trial; Montreal's mayor was interned for four years after he criticized conscription policy, and more than 100 Communist Party leaders were imprisoned after the party was banned.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The Regulations took effect in the first days of Canada's involvement in the Second World War, one week before Canada's own declaration against Germany.
incidents.outcome_note: The Defence of Canada Regulations remained in force for the duration of the war and were replaced by similar legislation on December 31, 1945.
